claims.text: BMW states its Neue Klasse (Gen6) uses an 800‑volt electrical architecture and that Gen6 high‑voltage batteries will provide about 30% faster charging and up to 30% greater WLTP range versus the previous generation.

BMW says the Neue Klasse’s new cylindrical Gen6 cell has roughly 20% greater energy density than BMW’s prior Gen5 prismatic cell, a change BMW links directly to the stated range and charging improvements.

BMW’s March 2025 media information for the BMW i5 (G60) shows that the G60 uses a 400‑volt battery architecture and a maximum DC fast‑charging power of 205 kW (10–80% in ~30 minutes), providing a 2025 technical baseline for the 5‑series‑segment sedan.

IEA’s Global EV Outlook 2026 notes the industry trend toward higher‑voltage architectures and faster charging: in 2025 about 160 BEV models supported >150 kW charging, only ~50 supported >250 kW, and the report explains that higher‑voltage systems (e.g., 800V) reduce charging time — supporting the expectation more premium models will support faster charging through 2028–2031.

The Joint Office of Energy and Transportation documents that SAE published a J3400 Technical Information Report in December 2023 and that most vehicle manufacturers announced plans to adopt the J3400/NACS connector beginning as early as 2025, which enables broader cross‑network connector compatibility in North America.
claims.publisher: U.S. Joint Office of Energy and Transportation

claims.text: General Motors says it expects all GM EVs to ship with a native NACS charging port by the 2027 model year, a step that increases mainstream non‑Tesla access to Tesla Superchargers in the US from 2027 onward.

claims.text: EVgo’s SEC filing and investor materials state the company is building out GM‑funded fast‑charger stalls (2,850 stalls to be installed by June 30, 2028) and reported pilots/rollouts of NACS/J3400 connectors and plans for higher‑power (350 kW and higher) stalls as part of its network expansion.
claims.about: charging network expansion and high‑power chargers through 2028

claims.text: The NEVI Formula Program (Bipartisan Infrastructure Law) and related federal guidance aimed to help fund a nationwide public fast‑charging build‑out (the broader goal tied to ~500,000 public chargers by 2030), but FHWA/NEVI guidance was revised in August 2025 to give states more flexibility on spacing (the earlier ‘every 50 miles’ shorthand is therefore not a fixed mandate for all states going forward).
